question: My study permit expired before I applied for my PGWP. What can I do?
answer:
If your study permit expired before you applied for your PGWP, you have two options:

1. Apply for a visitor record to stay in Canada longer.
2. Leave Canada and apply for your PGWP.

If you stay in Canada and let your permit expire, you must apply to restore your status as a student to apply for your PGWP. To restore your status, you must pay additional fees. (Source: Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html)

question: What is the difference between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit?
answer:
An employer-specific work permit lets you work in Canada under the conditions of the permit until the expiry date, with details such as the employer, location, and occupation listed on the permit. (Source: Employer-specific work permits: eligibility, LMIA, and application steps, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employer-specific.html)

An open work permit, on the other hand, lets you work for any employer in Canada, except those who are on the non-compliant list or regularly offer striptease, erotic dance, or escort services, or erotic massages. You don’t need a job offer to apply for an open work permit. (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html)

question: What is an LMIA and when does my employer need one?
answer: An LMIA (Labour Market Impact Assessment) is a document that proves there’s a need to hire a foreign worker to fill the job. Most jobs need an LMIA. question: How long can my parents stay in Canada with a super visa?
answer:
If you entered Canada before June 22, 2023, your parents can stay in Canada for the length of time the border officer granted them when they entered Canada, which can be up to 2 years. However, they can apply to extend their stay or leave Canada before the end of their authorized stay and re-enter Canada. (Source: Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

If your parents entered Canada on or after June 22, 2023, they are eligible to stay for 5 years at a time. (Source: Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

question: Who is eligible to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada?
answer:
To sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada, the sponsor must meet certain requirements. The sponsor must be at least 18 years old, be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and meet the income requirements for the sponsor. The sponsor must also not be inadmissible to Canada.

The person being sponsored must be at least 18 years old, be in a genuine relationship with the sponsor, and not be inadmissible to Canada. For a common-law partner, they must have lived with the sponsor for at least 12 consecutive months, with any time spent apart being short and temporary.

(Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)

question: If I can't sponsor my parents for permanent residence, how else can they come to Canada for long stays?
answer: If you can't sponsor your parents for permanent residence, they may be eligible to apply for a super visa which lets them stay in Canada for 5 years at a time. They can also apply for 2-year extensions to their stay while they’re still in Canada. question: What happens at the citizenship ceremony?
answer:
At the citizenship ceremony, you will:

- Take the oath of citizenship
- Reflect on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship
- Celebrate with your family and friends
- Receive your Canadian citizenship certificate (if you confirm that you want a paper certificate) or be told when your e-certificate will be available (Source: Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)
